items.text: Anchor bookcases, dressers, and the TV to the wall
items.note: Furniture tip-overs are a leading home injury for toddlers.

items.text: Cover unused electrical outlets with safety plugs
Install safety gates at the top and bottom of stairs
Add cabinet and drawer latches, especially where cleaning products or knives live
Move all medicines, cleaning products, and chemicals up high and locked away
Fit stove knob covers and turn pot handles toward the back
Secure blind and curtain cords out of reach
items.note: Looped cords are a strangulation hazard.

items.text: Pad sharp furniture corners and edges
Set your water heater to 49°C / 120°F to prevent scalds
Keep small objects, button batteries, and magnets off the floor and out of reach
items.note: Button batteries are a medical emergency if swallowed.

items.text: Use door-knob covers or locks on rooms that are off-limits
Check that smoke and carbon-monoxide alarms work, on every level
Keep the crib clear of pillows, bumpers, and toys, and away from windows and cords
Latch the toilet lid and keep the bathroom door closed
Tuck away or cover trailing electrical cords
Move toxic houseplants out of reach, or remove them
Crawl each room at your baby's eye level to spot hazards you'd miss standing up
Save poison-control and emergency numbers where everyone can find them
Car seat (infant or convertible), rear-facing and correctly rated
items.note: The one item you cannot skip.

items.text: Stroller or travel system that fits your car seat
Crib or bassinet with a firm, flat mattress and 2-4 fitted sheets
Swaddles and sleep sacks
6-8 bodysuits and sleepers each in 0-3 and 3-6 months
items.note: Register the bigger sizes too — newborn is outgrown fast.

Changing pad and a diaper caddy or diaper bag
Feeding gear: bottles and teats, plus a breast pump or nursing pillow if breastfeeding
Burp cloths, bibs, and muslins

A baby monitor

A few developmental toys, board books, and a play mat
Blackout blinds or a night light
A comfortable feeding chair, or a spot set up for feeds
Gift cards or a "cash fund" for big-ticket items and post-birth needs
items.note: Practical, and easy for guests.

items.text: 4-6 diapers, more for a long day out
items.note: Roughly one per hour out, plus a couple of spares.

items.text: A travel pack of wipes
A portable, foldable changing mat
Diaper cream in a small tube
Scented bags for dirty diapers
1-2 full changes of clothes for baby

items.text: Muslins or burp cloths
Feeding supplies: a bottle and formula, or a nursing cover if you prefer one
A bib and a few napkins
A pacifier or two, in a clean case
Hand sanitizer and a few tissues
A small first-aid kit: a thermometer, plasters, and infant paracetamol

items.text: Sun hat and baby-safe sunscreen in summer, or an extra layer and hat in winter
A light blanket or swaddle
A small toy or two to distract a fussy baby
A snack and water for you
items.note: Parents forget themselves.

items.text: A spare shirt for you

items.text: Restock it after every outing so it's always ready to grab
Photo ID, insurance details, and your hospital notes or birth plan
A comfortable, loose nightgown or two

Several pairs of high-waisted, disposable, or old underwear

Toiletries: toothbrush, toothpaste, lip balm, hair ties, and travel-size wash

If breastfeeding: nursing bras, breast pads, nipple cream, and a pump if you'll express

Burp cloths and bibs

Baby bath support, hooded towels, and fragrance-free baby wash

A stack of muslin cloths for everything

Contact details for your pediatrician and the out-of-hours line
Warm layers, a hat, and mittens if the weather's cold

items.note: Caring for yourself is part of the first month.

items.text: Nail your positioning: who it's for, the problem it solves, and why it's different
items.note: Everything downstream — copy, pricing, targeting — flows from this one paragraph.

items.text: Define the launch goal and the metrics you'll judge it by (signups, revenue, installs)
Set the launch date and work backward into a dated pre-launch timeline
Run a private beta and collect feedback, testimonials, and bug reports
Fix the launch-blocking issues from beta and confirm the release candidate
Finalize pricing, packaging, and any launch-day offer or trial
Write the core messaging and prepare the landing or product page
Prepare launch assets: demo video, screenshots, press kit, and FAQ
Line up distribution: email list, social posts, communities, and any press or creators
items.note: Warm your audience with teasers before launch day, not on it.

items.text: Set up analytics, event tracking, and dashboards to measure the launch
items.note: Verify events fire in a staging environment before launch day.

items.text: Brief support and sales, and prepare canned answers to the likely questions
Do a full dry run: test signup, checkout, onboarding, and the support path end to end
Schedule the launch-day posts, emails, and any submission (directory, marketplace, or press embargo)
Launch: publish the page, send the announcement, and post across your channels
Monitor systems, error rates, and payments closely for the first hours
Engage in real time: reply to comments, questions, and reviews as they come in
Track results against your launch metrics and note what converted best
Follow up with leads, trials, and press who engaged but didn't convert
Gather feedback from new users and triage the first round of fixes
Run a launch retrospective: what worked, what didn't, and what to repeat next time
Write a simple business plan: what you sell, to whom, and how you'll make money
Choose a business structure (sole trader, LLC, partnership, or company)
items.note: It affects your tax, paperwork, and personal liability — ask an accountant if you're unsure.

items.text: Pick and check your business name for availability and trademark conflicts
Register the business with the relevant government authority
Register for tax and get any required tax ID or number
Check which licenses or permits your trade and location require
items.note: Requirements vary a lot by industry and region — don't assume you need none.

items.text: Open a dedicated business bank account
Set up bookkeeping or accounting software from day one
Get the business insurance your trade needs (liability, professional, contents)
Set up a system to track income, expenses, and receipts for tax time
Choose how you'll take payment: card reader, online checkout, or invoicing
Set your prices and payment terms, and prepare an invoice template
Register a domain and set up a professional email address
Build a simple website or listing so customers can find and contact you
Set up the tools you'll run the business on (calendar, storage, comms)
Sort out suppliers, stock, or the equipment you need to deliver
Understand your record-keeping and tax-filing deadlines
Do a soft launch to test your systems before you open fully
Tie the post to a goal: awareness, engagement, traffic, or conversion
Lead with a strong hook in the first line or frame
items.note: Feeds are scrolled fast; the first line decides whether anyone reads the rest.

items.text: Deliver one clear idea or piece of value per post
Match the format to the platform (aspect ratio, length, and style)
Write in the platform's native voice, not one caption copied across all of them
Add a clear call to action — comment, save, share, or click
Include high-quality visuals or video sized correctly for the platform
Add captions or subtitles to any video
items.note: Most video is watched on mute.

items.text: Add descriptive alt text to images for accessibility and reach
Use a focused set of relevant hashtags, not a generic wall of them
Check that any link works and is tracked with a UTM or short link
Tag relevant people, brands, or locations where it adds value
Proofread for spelling, grammar, and factual accuracy
Confirm you have the rights to any image, music, or clip you've used
Schedule the post for when your audience is actually active
Cross-post or adapt the content for other channels where it fits
Plan to reply to comments and DMs within the first hour or two
items.note: Early engagement signals the algorithm to show the post more widely.

items.text: Log the post so you can review what performed and repeat what worked
Write down the problem you're solving and who has it most painfully
items.note: A startup that solves a real, urgent problem beats a clever idea nobody needs.

items.text: Talk to 20-30 potential customers before building anything
Research the market size, the competitors, and how people solve this today
Define your unique value: why you, why now, and why different
Test demand with a landing page, waitlist, or pre-sale before you build
Sketch a business model: how you make money and what it costs to deliver
Choose a business structure and register the company
Sort the legal basics: licenses, contracts, terms, and a privacy policy
Open a business bank account and set up bookkeeping
items.note: Keep business and personal money separate from day one.

items.text: Secure the name: domain, a trademark check, and social handles
Build a minimum viable product — the smallest thing that solves the core problem
Set up basic branding: a logo, colours, and a simple one-page website
Get a few pilot users onto the MVP and gather honest feedback
Iterate on the product until users see clear, repeatable value
Set pricing based on value and what the market will bear
Set up payments, invoicing, and the tools to fulfill or deliver
Plan how you'll reach customers: the one or two channels you'll focus on
Launch to your waitlist and first target audience
Land your first paying customers and learn from every objection
Track your key numbers and decide what to double down on or change
Proofread every page for typos, broken sentences, and leftover placeholder text
Test every link, button, and navigation menu for dead ends
items.note: Broken internal links hurt both users and crawlers.

items.text: Check the site on real phones, tablets, and desktop, and across the major browsers
Confirm all images have alt text and are compressed for fast loading
Set up and test every form, and confirm submissions arrive where they should
Add page titles, meta descriptions, and Open Graph tags to each page
Create and submit an XML sitemap and a robots.txt file
Set canonical URLs and resolve any duplicate-content issues
Install analytics and confirm events and conversions actually fire
items.note: Test in a real browser, not just the tag preview.

items.text: Run a performance audit and fix slow-loading pages and oversized assets
Confirm HTTPS is enforced and the SSL certificate is valid
Set up 301 redirects from every old URL to its new equivalent
items.note: Skipping redirects on a redesign is the fastest way to lose your rankings.

items.text: Add a custom 404 page and test that it works
Check accessibility: colour contrast, keyboard navigation, and heading structure
Back up the site and confirm you can actually restore it
Configure security: firewall, spam protection, and two-factor auth on admin
Point the domain and DNS, and confirm the site resolves on www and non-www
Go live, then immediately test the homepage, the checkout or contact path, and the forms
Submit the site to search engines and request indexing of the key pages
Monitor analytics, error logs, and uptime for the first days, and fix what breaks
Make the beds as soon as everyone is up
items.note: A made bed makes the whole room read as tidy.

items.text: Wash the dishes, or load and run the dishwasher, after each meal
Wipe down the kitchen counters and the hob after cooking
Clear and wipe the dining table once the plates are gone
Do a 10-minute tidy: put stray items back where they belong, room by room
Wipe the bathroom sink and taps, and squeegee the shower after use
items.note: A quick squeegee stops limescale and mould building up.

items.text: Run, hang, or fold one load of laundry to stop it piling up
Sweep or spot-vacuum the kitchen floor for crumbs and spills
Take out the kitchen bin if it's full, and reset a fresh liner
Wipe down high-touch spots: door handles, light switches, and taps
Sort the day's post and paperwork so it doesn't pile up
Empty pockets, and put shoes, coats, and bags away by the door
Give the toilet a quick brush and wipe the seat
Fluff the sofa cushions and fold any blankets before bed
Set out what you need for the morning, and give the sink a final wipe
Dust from the top down: light fixtures, ceiling corners, and the tops of doorframes and wardrobes
items.note: Dust falls, so always start high and finish at the floor.

items.text: Wash walls, switch plates, and skirting boards with a damp microfiber cloth
Clean windows inside and out, including the tracks and sills
items.note: A cotton bud lifts the grime packed into the corners of the tracks.

items.text: Launder the curtains and wipe down blinds slat by slat
Descale the kettle and coffee machine with a vinegar or citric-acid solution
Degrease the extractor hood and soak or replace its filter
items.note: Metal filters can go through a hot dishwasher cycle.

items.text: Deep-clean the oven: remove the racks to soak, and scrub the interior glass
Pull out the fridge, defrost the freezer, and wipe the coils and door seals
Empty and wipe every kitchen cupboard, checking food dates while you're in there
Run an empty hot cycle with cleaner in the washing machine and dishwasher
items.note: Wipe the rubber door seal and clear the dishwasher filter.

items.text: Scrub the grout and re-caulk any mouldy sealant around the bath and sink
Descale the showerhead by soaking it in vinegar overnight
Disinfect and descale the toilet, including the base and behind the bowl
Vacuum and flip the mattresses, and wash mattress protectors and pillows
Wash or dry-clean duvets, and vacuum the divan or bed base
Move furniture to vacuum underneath, then shampoo carpets or mop hard floors
Wipe down radiators and vacuum the dust from between the fins
Disinfect high-touch spots: light switches, door handles, and remote controls
Vacuum upholstered sofas and chairs, including under the cushions
Empty, wash, and disinfect every bin, including the kitchen caddy
Daily: wash up or run the dishwasher after meals
Daily: wipe the kitchen counters and the hob
Daily: make the beds and do a quick tidy of each room
Daily: take out the kitchen bin when full and reset the liner
Weekly: change and wash the bed sheets and pillowcases
items.note: Weekly in summer; every two weeks is fine in winter.

items.text: Weekly: vacuum all carpets and rugs, and mop the hard floors
Weekly: clean the bathroom — toilet, sink, bath, shower, and mirror
Weekly: dust the surfaces, shelves, and electronics throughout
Weekly: wipe the kitchen appliance fronts, the microwave, and the sink
Weekly: do the full laundry, including towels and tea towels
Weekly: empty and wipe out all the household bins
Weekly: water the houseplants and clear away any dead leaves
Monthly: wipe down skirting boards, door handles, and light switches
Monthly: clean the oven and degrease the extractor hood
items.note: Doing it monthly stops grease baking on and needing a deep scrub.

items.text: Monthly: descale the kettle, coffee machine, and showerhead
Monthly: wash the bins, doormats, and any pet bedding
Monthly: run a hot maintenance cycle in the washing machine and dishwasher
Monthly: clean the windows and wipe the sills
Monthly: vacuum under the furniture and behind large appliances
Monthly: check and restock cleaning supplies, and replace worn sponges and cloths
Start once the place is empty: open the windows, and gather bin bags, cloths, and cleaners before you begin
Kitchen first: empty every cupboard and drawer, then wipe them inside and out
Deep-clean the oven, hob, grill, and extractor filter
items.note: Grease inside the oven is the single most-docked item on an inventory.

items.text: Defrost, empty, and wipe the fridge and freezer, and leave the doors ajar if you're switching them off
Descale the kettle, and clean the sink, taps, and any tiled splashback
Bathroom next: descale the toilet, taps, and showerhead, and scrub limescale off the screen
Clean and re-whiten the grout, and wipe mould off the silicone sealant
items.note: A dab of mould remover left for an hour lifts black spotting.

items.text: Polish the mirrors, chrome, and glass until they're streak-free
Wipe down all interior doors, handles, and light switches
Clean the inside and outside of every window, plus the sills and tracks
Dust and wipe skirting boards, radiators, and picture rails throughout
Remove cobwebs from ceiling corners and light fittings in every room
Fill nail holes and wipe scuffs off the walls
items.note: Check your tenancy agreement on whether small holes need filling.

items.text: Wipe inside all built-in wardrobes and storage cupboards
Clean any supplied appliances — the washing machine drawer, dishwasher filter, and microwave
Take a full set of dated photos once each room is done, as proof of its condition
Vacuum every room, including inside the cupboards and along the edges
Mop the hard floors and shampoo or spot-clean the carpets, working toward the front door last
Open every window to air out the whole home before you start
Declutter room by room, sorting into keep, donate, sell, and bin piles
items.note: Declutter first — there's no point cleaning around things you're getting rid of.

items.text: Wash the windows inside and out, and clean the tracks, sills, and screens
Launder or dry-clean the curtains, and dust the blinds slat by slat
Take down and wash light fittings and lampshades, and replace any dead bulbs
Dust ceiling corners, cornices, and the tops of doorframes and wardrobes
Wipe walls, skirting boards, switch plates, and door handles
Vacuum and flip the mattresses, and wash duvets, pillows, and protectors
items.note: A sunny, breezy day is ideal for airing bedding outside.

items.text: Swap the wardrobe over to the new season, and donate what didn't get worn
Empty, wipe, and reorganize kitchen cupboards, checking food dates as you go
Deep-clean the oven, and degrease the extractor hood and its filter
Defrost the freezer, and wipe the fridge shelves and door seals
Descale the kettle, coffee machine, and showerhead
Scrub the bathroom grout and refresh any discoloured sealant
Wipe down radiators and clear the dust from between the fins
Clean behind and underneath the heavy furniture and appliances
Shampoo carpets and rugs, and mop and polish the hard floors
Wipe the front and inside of every kitchen appliance and small gadget
Clean and disinfect the bins, and replace worn cloths and sponges
Tackle one outdoor job: sweep the patio, wash the doormat, or clean the bins
Workout clothes: a moisture-wicking top and shorts or leggings
items.note: Sweat-wicking fabric beats cotton, which stays wet and chafes.

items.text: Proper training shoes for your workout
A spare pair of socks
Water bottle
items.note: Fill it before you leave so you're not queuing at the fountain.

items.text: Small sweat towel for wiping down equipment and yourself
Padlock for the locker
Headphones, charged
Lifting gloves or wrist straps, if you lift heavy
A resistance band for warm-ups and activation
A pre- or post-workout snack or protein shake
items.note: Protein plus carbs within an hour or two of training supports recovery.

items.text: Deodorant
Shower kit: travel soap or body wash, shampoo, and flip-flops
items.note: Flip-flops keep you off shared shower floors.

items.text: A quick-dry towel for showering
A full change of clean clothes and underwear
A dry bag or plastic bag for sweaty clothes
items.note: Keeps the wet kit from soaking everything else in the bag.

items.text: Membership card or the gym app on your phone
Hair ties or a headband
Phone plus a charger or power bank
Get a medical check-up before you start, especially if you're new to running or have any health concerns
Buy properly fitted running shoes, ideally after a gait analysis at a running store
items.note: The wrong shoes are the fastest route to injury over hundreds of training miles.

items.text: Choose a 16 to 20 week training plan that matches your current fitness
items.note: Beginners need the full 20 weeks; don't rush a compressed plan.

items.text: Set a realistic goal: to finish, or a specific target time
Base phase (weeks 1 to 4): build easy, conversational mileage running 3 to 4 times a week
Add one weekly long run and increase its distance gradually
items.note: Raise weekly mileage by no more than about 10% to avoid overuse injuries.

items.text: Include one speed or tempo session each week to build pace
Strength-train twice a week, focusing on core, glutes, and legs
Cross-train on off days with cycling or swimming to build fitness without pounding
Dial in your race-day nutrition and practice fueling on long runs
items.note: Never try a new gel or drink on race day — test everything in training.

items.text: Prioritize hydration, sleep, and recovery throughout the block
Peak weeks: reach your longest run of about 20 miles (32 km) around 3 weeks out
Taper: cut your mileage over the final 2 to 3 weeks so you arrive fresh
items.note: Resist the urge to cram fitness late — the work is already done.

items.text: Lay out your race-day gear the night before, using nothing new
items.note: Wear only clothes and shoes you've already run long in.

items.text: Carb-load and hydrate well over the final few days
Race day: start slower than feels easy and stick to your pace and fueling plan
items.note: Going out too fast is the classic first-marathon mistake.

items.text: After the race: keep moving to cool down, refuel, hydrate, and rest before running again
items.note: Give yourself at least a week of easy recovery before hard training resumes.

items.text: Pick 2 to 3 recipes that reheat well
items.note: Stews, grain bowls, roasted veg, and curries hold up far better than salads or crispy foods.

items.text: Plan the week's meals: breakfasts, lunches, dinners, and snacks
Check what you already have in the fridge, freezer, and pantry
Write a shopping list grouped by store section
items.note: Grouping by aisle turns the shop into one fast lap.

items.text: Do a single grocery run for the whole week
Wash and chop all your vegetables at once
Cook grains and starches in bulk: rice, quinoa, pasta, or potatoes
Batch-cook proteins: chicken, ground meat, beans, tofu, or hard-boiled eggs
Roast a big tray of mixed vegetables
Make one sauce or dressing to vary the flavor across meals
items.note: The same base tastes new with pesto one day and a peanut sauce the next.

items.text: Portion meals into containers and label each with the date
Cool food fully before sealing the lids
items.note: Sealing warm food traps steam, goes soggy, and spoils faster.

items.text: Freeze any portions you won't eat within 3 to 4 days
items.note: Cooked meals keep about 3 to 4 days in the fridge; freeze the rest.

items.text: Prep grab-and-go snacks: cut fruit, portioned nuts, or yogurt cups
Arrange the fridge by day or meal so the right container is easy to grab
Clean as you go and wash your containers so next week is easy
Wake at a consistent time and get up without hitting snooze
items.note: A steady wake time anchors your whole body clock, even on weekends.

items.text: Get bright light within 30 to 60 minutes: open the curtains or step outside
items.note: Morning daylight is the strongest signal for alertness and better sleep that night.

items.text: Drink a large glass of water
items.note: You wake up mildly dehydrated after 7 to 8 hours without fluids.

items.text: Make your bed
Move your body for 5 to 10 minutes: stretch, walk, or a light workout
Brush your teeth and wash your face, or splash with cold water to wake up
Do 5 minutes of breathing, meditation, or quiet before the noise starts
Write your top 3 priorities for the day
items.note: Deciding what matters before you open email keeps the day on your terms.

items.text: Eat a protein-forward breakfast
items.note: Protein keeps you full and steadies energy better than a sugary start.

items.text: Take any vitamins or supplements
Delay caffeine until about 90 minutes after waking
items.note: It smooths out the mid-morning crash — optional, but many people notice the difference.

items.text: Shower and get dressed
Review your calendar and to-do list for the day
Keep your phone and email out of the first 30 to 60 minutes
items.note: Starting on your own priorities beats reacting to everyone else's.

items.text: Drink enough water through the day
Get 7 to 9 hours of sleep
items.note: A consistent bedtime and wake time matters as much as the hours.

items.text: Move your body for 20 to 30 minutes, even just a walk
Eat at least one balanced, home-cooked meal
Step outside for fresh air and daylight
Take a real break from screens
items.note: Even 20 minutes away from a screen resets your focus.

items.text: Do one thing purely because you enjoy it
Connect with a friend or someone you love
items.note: A short call or message counts — connection is a core need, not a luxury.

items.text: Write down 3 things you're grateful for
Tidy one small space to clear your head
Say no to one thing that drains you
items.note: Protecting your energy is self-care, not selfishness.

items.text: Do a 5-minute breathing or meditation session
Stretch or take a warm bath to release tension
Set a limit on doomscrolling and social media
Take any medications or supplements you need
Plan something small to look forward to
Check in with yourself: how am I actually feeling today?
items.note: Naming an emotion takes the edge off it.

Peppers, carrots, and cucumber for snacking

Avocados

Whole-grain bread or wraps

Oats and a breakfast cereal
Flour — all-purpose, plus any you bake with
Breadcrumbs or a stuffing mix
Canned tomatoes — whole and chopped
items.note: The base of countless quick dinners.

items.text: Canned beans, chickpeas, and lentils
Canned tuna, and coconut milk for curries
Stock cubes or bouillon
items.note: Turns water into the base of soups, rice, and sauces.

items.text: Pasta sauce, and a jar of pesto or curry paste
Peanut butter, and a jam or honey
Cooking oil and olive oil
Vinegar — white, plus a balsamic or wine vinegar
Soy sauce, hot sauce, and Worcestershire or fish sauce
Ketchup, mustard, and mayonnaise
Salt, black pepper, and a pepper mill
Everyday spices — cumin, paprika, chili, cinnamon, and mixed herbs
items.note: Buy the ones you actually cook with, not a giant rack that goes stale.

items.text: Garlic and onion powder, plus a stock of fresh garlic and onions
Sugar — white and brown — plus baking soda and baking powder
Vanilla extract, and a bar of chocolate or cocoa
Coffee, tea, and long-life or powdered milk as a backup
Nuts, dried fruit, and a couple of snack bars
items.note: Store opened nuts sealed — they go rancid over time.

items.text: A mix of soft drinks, juice, and sparkling water
items.note: Plan about 2-3 drinks per guest for the first few hours.

items.text: Beer, wine, or a batch cocktail, if you're serving alcohol
Plenty of ice — more than you think you'll need
items.note: Roughly 1-2 lbs (0.5-1 kg) per guest for drinks and coolers.

items.text: Coffee, tea, and milk for later in the night
A main or two — a platter, tray bake, pizzas, or something on the grill
Buns, bread, or wraps if you're serving anything handheld
A couple of dips — hummus, salsa, guacamole, or a cheese dip
Chips, crackers, pretzels, and nuts for grazing
items.note: Set snacks out before guests arrive to cover the early lull.

items.text: A cheese and charcuterie board — cheeses, cured meats, and crackers
A veggie platter and fruit for lighter and dietary options
items.note: Always include a vegetarian and a non-alcoholic option.

items.text: Dessert — a cake, cookies, or something easy to serve
Condiments: ketchup, mustard, mayo, and any sauces your mains need
Paper plates, napkins, cups, and cutlery
items.note: Buy about 1.5x your guest count — plates and cups get swapped.

items.text: Serving bowls, platters, and a couple of serving spoons
Trash bags and a recycling bag, set out where guests can see them
Paper towels and cleaning wipes for spills
A cooler or two, plus bags of ice to fill them
Bottle opener, corkscrew, and a can opener
Aluminum foil, cling film, and containers for leftovers
Candles, a lighter, and music or a speaker for atmosphere
A few extras for allergies or kids — a gluten-free snack and a juice option
items.note: Ask guests about allergies when they RSVP.

items.text: Bananas, plus a couple of apples or oranges
Leafy greens — spinach, lettuce, or a salad mix
items.note: Buy loose if you'll use it fast; bagged wilts quicker.

items.text: Tomatoes, cucumber, and bell peppers
Onions, garlic, and potatoes
items.note: Store these cool and dark, and keep onions away from potatoes.

items.text: Carrots and a broccoli or seasonal vegetable
A bunch of fresh herbs and a lemon
Chicken breasts or thighs
Ground beef, turkey, or a plant-based mince
A dozen eggs
Fish, or canned tuna or salmon
Beans, chickpeas, or lentils, canned or dried
items.note: A cheap protein that stretches any meal.

items.text: Milk or a plant-based alternative
Butter and a block or wedge of cheese
Yogurt — plain or Greek
Bread, wraps, or bagels
Pasta, rice, or noodles
Cooking oil, plus salt, pepper, and a spice you're low on
Pasta sauce or canned tomatoes
Breakfast cereal or oats
Coffee, tea, or your morning drink
Frozen vegetables and a bag of frozen fruit for smoothies

items.text: Household basics you're low on — dish soap, paper towels, or trash bags
Redirect your mail with your postal service
items.note: Set it to start on your move date — it buys time to update everyone else.

items.text: File your official change of address with the government: voter roll, tax authority, and driver's license agency
Update your bank, credit cards, and any loan or mortgage providers
Tell your employer's payroll and HR, and update pension or retirement accounts
Update your insurance: home or renter's, car, health, and life policies
Switch or transfer utilities: electricity, gas, water, internet, and phone
Update your doctor, dentist, and pharmacy, and transfer prescriptions
Change your address on subscriptions and deliveries
items.note: Streaming billing, meal kits, Amazon, and any recurring boxes.

items.text: Update your driving license and vehicle registration
items.note: Many places require this within a set number of days.

items.text: Tell schools or childcare and transfer any records
Update online shopping accounts and digital wallets
Let friends and family know, and update your address on any wills or legal documents
Bed, mattress, pillows, and two sets of sheets
Bath towels, hand towels, and a shower curtain
A basic kitchen kit: pots, a pan, a chef's knife, a cutting board, and a can opener
Plates, bowls, glasses, mugs, and cutlery for four
items.note: Four covers guests without the clutter.

items.text: Cooking basics: spatula, wooden spoon, measuring cups, a mixing bowl, a colander
Food storage containers, foil, cling film, and bin bags
A microwave, kettle, or toaster if not already provided
Cleaning kit: all-purpose spray, dish soap, sponges, a mop, broom, and vacuum
Laundry basket, detergent, and a drying rack
Toilet paper, hand soap, and a plunger

items.text: A basic toolkit: hammer, screwdrivers, tape measure, and picture hooks
Extension leads and enough phone and laptop chargers
A first-aid kit and basic medicines
Working smoke and carbon-monoxide detectors

items.text: Trash and recycling bins
Light bulbs and a lamp or nightlight for each room
Renter's insurance and copies of your lease and inventory
items.note: Photograph any existing damage on day one.

items.text: A shower caddy, bath mat, and toothbrush holder
Pantry staples: salt, oil, pasta, coffee or tea
A doormat and a few command hooks for keys
Eight weeks out: set your moving date and budget, and decide between movers and a DIY van
items.note: Get three quotes before you book.

items.text: Seven weeks out: declutter room by room and sell, donate, or bin what you won't take
items.note: You pay to move everything, so lighten the load first.

items.text: Six weeks out: book your movers or hire van, and reserve any elevator or parking permits
items.note: Good movers book out early in summer.

items.text: Five weeks out: gather boxes, tape, bubble wrap, and markers, and start packing rarely-used rooms
Four weeks out: notify your landlord or list your home, and confirm your new address details
Three weeks out: transfer or set up utilities, internet, and insurance at the new place
items.note: Book the internet install early — slots fill up.

items.text: Two weeks out: file your change of address and redirect your mail
items.note: See our change-of-address checklist for who to tell.

items.text: One week out: pack everything but essentials, label boxes by room, and defrost the freezer
Two days out: pack an essentials box (chargers, toiletries, meds, a change of clothes) and keep it with you
Moving day: photograph meter readings, do a final walkthrough, and check every room and cupboard before you leave
First day in: find the fuse box, stopcock, and thermostat, and test that the utilities work
First week in: unpack essentials, update your address on IDs and accounts, and register with a local doctor
Locate and label the fuse box, water stopcock, and gas shut-off
items.note: You'll want these in an emergency, not during one.

items.text: Test smoke and carbon-monoxide alarms and replace any dead batteries
Take meter readings (gas, electric, water) and send them to your providers
Confirm utilities, heating, and hot water all work
Change the locks, or at least have the keys re-keyed
items.note: You don't know who else still has a copy.

items.text: Set up and test your internet and Wi-Fi
Do a deep clean before furniture arrives
items.note: Kitchen, bathroom, and floors are easiest empty.

items.text: Check for leaks, damp, or pest signs and photograph any issues for your records
Find the nearest hospital, pharmacy, and grocery store
Learn your bin and recycling collection days and where the bins go
Unpack your essentials box first: bedding, toiletries, chargers, and a kettle
Register with a local doctor and dentist
Introduce yourself to the neighbours and ask about parking and building quirks
Update your address on IDs, accounts, and deliveries
items.note: See the change-of-address checklist.

items.text: Set up a basic first-aid kit and a fire extinguisher
Note your landlord's or property manager's emergency contact
Program the thermostat and check every window and door lock
Plan your furniture layout before hauling heavy items around
Gather supplies: sturdy boxes in a few sizes, packing tape, bubble wrap, packing paper, and markers
Declutter first — donate, sell, or bin anything you won't use
items.note: Don't pay to move what you'll throw away.

items.text: Pack room by room, finishing one before you start the next
Label every box with its room and contents, and mark fragile boxes clearly
items.note: Label the sides, not the top — you'll stack them.

items.text: Keep boxes under about 15kg
items.note: Heavy items in small boxes, light items in big ones.

items.text: Wrap breakables individually and fill gaps so nothing shifts
Use towels, blankets, and clothing as padding to save on bubble wrap
Keep screws and small parts in labelled bags taped to the furniture they belong to
Photograph the back of your TV and electronics before unplugging them
Pack a "first night" essentials box and keep it with you
items.note: Bedding, toiletries, chargers, meds, snacks.

items.text: Pack a separate valuables bag: documents, jewellery, medications, and small electronics you carry yourself
Empty, clean, and dry appliances, and defrost the freezer at least a day ahead
Seal liquids in bags and pack them upright to stop leaks
Keep a "packing kit" of tape, scissors, and a marker you can always find
Leave clothes on hangers and slip a bin bag over them as a quick wardrobe box
Either empty drawers or wrap the whole unit closed — don't overpack them
Count and number your boxes so you know if any go missing
Load the truck with the heaviest items first and against the cab
Backpack that fits a laptop or binders comfortably
items.note: Padded straps matter if your books are heavy.

items.text: Spiral notebooks, or a binder with loose-leaf paper, for each subject
Pens in black and blue, pencils, and a good eraser
Highlighters in a few colors and a set of markers
Pencil case or pouch to keep it all in one place
Ruler, scissors, and a glue stick
Sticky notes, index cards, and paper clips
Folders or dividers to sort handouts by subject
items.note: One color per subject makes grabbing the right one automatic.

items.text: A planner or academic calendar for deadlines
items.note: Even with a phone, a paper planner is easy to glance at.

items.text: Scientific or graphing calculator, if your math class needs one
items.note: Check which model is allowed on tests.

items.text: Laptop or tablet and its charger
Headphones for library work and online lessons
USB drive or a cloud storage account for backups
Water bottle and a reusable lunch bag or box
Hand sanitizer and a small pack of tissues
Sticky tabs and a stapler for organizing notes
Whiteboard markers or a small dry-erase board for revision
A reusable tote for gym kit or extra books
A first-day kit: schedule, locker combo, ID, and a bit of cash
items.note: Have these ready the night before.

items.text: Twin XL sheets, a mattress topper, pillows, and a comforter
items.note: Most dorm beds are twin XL, not standard twin — check first.

items.text: Mattress protector and an extra set of sheets
Bath towels, a hand towel, and a quick-dry shower towel
Shower caddy and flip-flops for shared bathrooms
items.note: Flip-flops are non-negotiable in communal showers.

items.text: Toiletries, a toothbrush holder, and a refillable water bottle
Laptop, charger, and a padded sleeve or bag
Power strip with surge protection and a couple of extension cords
items.note: Dorm outlets are always too few and too far away.

items.text: Phone charger, headphones, and any adapters you need
Desk lamp and a small clip-on reading light
Notebooks, pens, highlighters, sticky notes, and a planner
Backpack for class and a reusable water bottle
Under-bed storage bins and a few drawer organizers
items.note: Vertical and under-bed space is where dorms hide extra room.

items.text: Laundry hamper, detergent pods, and a roll of quarters or a laundry card
Basic first-aid kit and any daily medications
items.note: Include pain relievers, bandages, and a thermometer.

items.text: Mini fridge or microwave — coordinate so you and your roommate don't both bring one
items.note: Message your roommate before move-in day.

items.text: A few mugs, plates, utensils, and a reusable food container
Command hooks, poster strips, and a small toolkit
items.note: Adhesive hooks save your deposit — no nails in dorm walls.

items.text: Fan, plus a warm blanket or throw for cold nights
Important documents: ID, insurance card, and a copy of your housing and class schedule
A little decor — photos, string lights, or a rug to make the room yours
Two weeks out: list every topic on the syllabus and mark each as strong, shaky, or not started
items.note: Be honest — the shaky ones need the most time.

items.text: Two weeks out: gather your notes, textbook, past papers, and the exam format and mark scheme
items.note: Know how many questions, how long, and what's weighted.

items.text: Two weeks out: build a revision timetable that gives weak topics more sessions than strong ones
12 days out: start with active recall — close the book and write what you remember, then check
items.note: Re-reading feels productive, but recall is what builds memory.

items.text: 10 days out: turn your weak topics into flashcards or a one-page summary each
items.note: Condensing forces you to understand, not just copy.

items.text: 9 days out: do your first past paper untimed, with notes, to find the gaps
7 days out: teach a tricky topic out loud to someone, or to an empty room
items.note: If you can explain it simply, you know it.

items.text: 6 days out: do a full past paper under real exam conditions and time yourself
items.note: Practice the pressure, not just the content.

items.text: 5 days out: mark your paper against the scheme and re-revise every question you lost marks on
4 days out: space short recall sessions across all topics rather than one long block
items.note: Spaced practice beats massed cramming.

items.text: 3 days out: memorize the formulas, dates, or definitions you still can't recall cold
2 days out: do a final timed paper, then review only your weakest two topics
Day before: pack your bag — ID, pens, calculator, water, and any permitted notes
items.note: Check the calculator batteries and any allowed materials.

items.text: Day before: confirm the exam time, room, and route, and set two alarms
items.note: Plan to arrive early enough to settle your nerves.

items.text: Day before: stop revising by early evening, eat well, and get a full night's sleep
items.note: Sleep consolidates memory better than one more hour of cramming.

items.text: Exam morning: eat breakfast, skim your one-page summaries, and arrive early
items.note: Light review only — no new material on the day.

items.text: Set a specific, measurable goal and its deadline
items.note: Pass the chemistry final on the 14th beats study more.

items.text: List every topic or chapter you need to cover
Rate each topic by how well you know it and how heavily it is weighted
items.note: Weak, high-weight topics get first claim on your time.

items.text: Estimate how many study sessions each topic needs
Look at your real week and find the hours you can protect for study
items.note: Plan around classes, work, and sleep — not on top of them.

items.text: Block those hours in a calendar as fixed appointments
items.note: A session with a time and a place is far more likely to happen.

items.text: Break study into focused blocks with short breaks, like 25 or 50 minutes on, then a rest
items.note: A steady on-off rhythm keeps focus from sagging.

items.text: Front-load weak topics early, while your energy and runway are highest
Build in spaced repetition — revisit each topic several times, not once
items.note: Spacing sessions out beats one long cram.

items.text: Choose an active method for each session: recall, past questions, or teaching it aloud
items.note: Doing beats re-reading every time.

items.text: Add buffer days for catch-up and the topics that run long
items.note: Something always takes longer than planned.

items.text: Track what you finish and check off each session as you go
items.note: Visible progress is its own motivation.

items.text: Review the plan weekly and shift time toward whatever is still shaky
Protect sleep, meals, and one rest day so you don't burn out
items.note: A rested brain retains more than an exhausted one.

items.text: Do a final review pass over everything a few days before the deadline
Choose and narrow your topic into a specific, answerable research question
items.note: Too broad is the number-one reason a thesis stalls.

items.text: Confirm your supervisor and agree on scope, expectations, and a rough timeline
Do a literature review and map what has already been written on your question
items.note: Note the gap your work will fill.

items.text: Write and get approval for your proposal or research plan
Choose your methodology and, if needed, get ethics or data approval
items.note: Ethics review can take weeks — start it early.

items.text: Set up a reference manager and log every source as you read
items.note: A citation manager saves days of cleanup later — set it up before you read.

items.text: Build a chapter outline with a target word count for each section
Collect and analyze your data or primary material
Draft the body chapters first — methods, results, and discussion
items.note: The introduction is easiest to write once you know what you found.

items.text: Write the introduction and literature review to frame the finished body
Write the conclusion, tying findings back to your original question
Write the abstract last, summarizing the whole thesis in one page
Revise for argument and structure — does each chapter earn its place?
items.note: Fix the big-picture flow before line-editing.

items.text: Proofread for grammar, and check every citation and reference for accuracy
Format to your department's guidelines: title page, contents, margins, and numbering
items.note: Follow the official template exactly — formatting rejections cost time.

items.text: Run a final plagiarism check and submit before the deadline, keeping a backup copy
items.note: Submit a day early to absorb any upload problems.

items.text: Passport, plus a printed and offline photo of your ID
items.note: Keep the copy separate from the original.

items.text: Visa or ETIAS authorization, if your nationality needs one
items.note: Check before you fly — approval isn't instant.

items.text: Two cards and about €50 in cash
items.note: Split them between bags in case one is lost.

items.text: Phone and a charger with an EU plug adapter
items.note: France uses Type C/E plugs at 230V.

items.text: Universal travel adapter
items.note: A back-up if your charger is US or UK only.

items.text: Comfortable, broken-in walking shoes
items.note: Paris is cobblestones — new shoes will blister.

items.text: Five layerable tops and two bottoms
items.note: Mix-and-match neutrals cut the volume.

items.text: A light jacket or trench
items.note: Paris evenings are cool even in summer.

items.text: Compact umbrella
items.note: Rain is common and unpredictable.

items.text: Crossbody anti-theft bag with a zip
items.note: Pickpockets work the Metro and the queues at big landmarks.

items.text: Reusable water bottle
items.note: Refill free at the city's Wallace fountains.

items.text: Pre-booked Louvre and Eiffel Tower tickets, or a Paris Museum Pass
items.note: Skip-the-line — they sell out in peak season.

items.text: Metro (RATP) app and an offline map
items.note: Download the map before you land.

items.text: A translation app and a few basic French phrases
items.note: A "bonjour" first goes a long way.

items.text: Daily medications and a small first-aid kit
items.note: Bring enough for the whole trip plus a spare day.

items.text: Sunglasses
Portable power bank
items.note: A day of maps and photos will drain your phone.

items.text: Toiletries in a clear bag, packed for 3 days
items.note: Plan one laundry run or a quick sink wash.

items.text: Passport or ID and travel documents
Two or three swimsuits

items.text: Reef-safe sunscreen SPF 30+ and after-sun

items.text: Wide-brim hat and UV-protection sunglasses
Lightweight cover-up or kaftan
Flip-flops plus one pair of walking sandals
Quick-dry beach towel

items.text: Breathable, light clothing for hot days
One warm layer for air-conditioned restaurants and evenings
Aloe vera or after-sun for sunburn
Insect repellent

items.text: Waterproof phone pouch and a dry bag for valuables
Refillable water bottle

items.text: Beach bag or tote
Daily medications plus motion-sickness tablets for boat trips
Basic first-aid: plasters, antiseptic, painkillers
Portable fan or cooling towel for extreme heat
Snorkel gear if you have it

items.text: E-reader or book with a waterproof case
Power bank and travel adapter
Photo ID or passport and any visa needed
Boarding passes, hotel, and rental-car confirmations
Laptop, charger, and a spare charging cable
Phone, power bank, and adapter for your destination
Business cards
Notebook and pens, or a tablet and stylus
Two or three wrinkle-resistant business outfits

items.text: One smart-casual outfit for dinners or downtime
Comfortable dress shoes you've already worn in
Toiletries and a grooming kit in travel sizes
Presentation dongles and an HDMI or USB-C adapter

items.text: Printed copies of key documents as a backup
Daily medications and basic painkillers
Reusable water bottle and a few snacks
Noise-cancelling headphones for the flight and the hotel
Expense receipts folder or app set up before you go
A small multi-port charger

items.text: A light layer for cold conference rooms and planes

items.text: Visa, ETA, or ETIAS for your destination

Travel insurance details and an emergency contact card

items.text: A change of clothes and essentials in your carry-on

items.text: Offline maps and a translation app downloaded before you fly

ID or passport and your booking confirmations
items.note: Screenshot them in case there's no signal.

items.text: Phone charger and a power bank
Two-to-three days of clothes in one color family
items.note: Everything mixes, nothing is wasted.

items.text: One "nice" outfit for dinner out
Pajamas, plus fresh socks and underwear per day and one spare
A light layer — sweater or jacket — for evenings
Comfortable walking shoes, plus one dressier pair
Toiletries in travel-size bottles under 100ml
items.note: The cabin liquid limit for carry-on.

items.text: Toothbrush, toothpaste, deodorant, and skincare
Daily medications, painkillers, and plasters
Sunglasses and, if sunny, sunscreen
Reusable water bottle
Chargers and cables for every device
A book, headphones, or downloaded shows for the journey
A small day bag or tote for outings
House keys and a card for parking or transit
A foldable tote or laundry bag for dirty clothes
Set the date, start and end time, and a rough guest count
Set a budget and split it across food, cake, decor, and entertainment
Pick a theme or color scheme
items.note: A theme makes every other choice — invites, decor, cake — easier.

items.text: Choose and book the venue, or prep your home

items.text: Send invitations 3 to 4 weeks ahead with an RSVP date

items.text: Plan the menu: food, drinks, and any dietary or allergy needs

items.text: Plan decorations: balloons, banner, tablecloth, and centerpieces
Plan activities and entertainment: games, a playlist, or a photo backdrop
Buy party favors or goodie bags
Buy or wrap the birthday gift

Prep a music playlist and test the speaker
Charge your phone or camera for photos
Day-of: set up 1 to 2 hours early, chill the drinks, and set out food just before guests arrive
Assign someone to greet guests and someone to manage the cake and candles moment

items.text: Define the event's goal and how you'll measure success

items.text: Set the date and hold a backup date
Set the budget and set up a simple way to track spending against it
Estimate the headcount and build the guest or attendee list
Book the venue and confirm its capacity and layout
Confirm exactly what the venue includes: tables, chairs, AV, wifi, parking
Hire the caterer and confirm dietary and allergy options

items.text: Arrange AV: sound, microphones, projector, and screens

items.text: Book speakers, entertainment, or a host, and confirm their needs
Build the run-of-show: a minute-by-minute timeline for the day
Send invitations or open registration, and track RSVPs
Plan decor, signage, and any branding or printed materials
Sort transportation, directions, and parking for attendees
Confirm permits, licenses, and event insurance

items.text: Line up staff or volunteers and give each a clear role
Prepare a day-of contact sheet with every vendor and lead's number
Plan cleanup, teardown, and who returns rentals
After the event: send thank-yous and gather feedback while it's fresh
Pick the occasion, date, and start and end time
Set a headcount and a budget
Choose a venue or prep your own space
Send invites 2 to 3 weeks ahead with an RSVP request
items.note: A group chat or a quick form is enough for a casual party.

items.text: Plan the menu and quantities, allowing for dietary needs
items.note: Ask about allergies and vegetarians when people RSVP.

items.text: Plan drinks: alcoholic and non-alcoholic, plus plenty of ice

items.text: Write a shopping list and shop 1 to 2 days ahead
Plan decor and lighting for the mood you want

items.text: Build a playlist long enough to cover the whole night, and test the speaker
Plan one activity or icebreaker if guests won't all know each other
Arrange seating and flow so people naturally mingle
Stock essentials: cups, plates, napkins, serving utensils, and trash bags
Clear space and set up a spot for coats and bags
Day-of: cook and prep early, chill the drinks, and give the bathroom a quick tidy
Ask a friend to co-host: manage the door and keep drinks and food topped up
Set out food about 15 minutes before guests are due
items.note: First guests always arrive right on time — be ready.

items.text: 8:00 am — Light breakfast, hydrate, and shower
items.note: Eat something real; it's a long day and the next full meal is dinner.

items.text: 9:00 am — Hair and makeup begins for the wedding party
items.note: The person getting married goes last so the look is freshest for photos.

items.text: 11:00 am — Photographer arrives for detail shots: rings, dress, invitations, shoes
12:00 pm — Getting-ready photos; the wedding party gets dressed
12:30 pm — Light lunch and drinks for everyone getting ready
1:00 pm — Get into the dress or suit with help on hand for buttons and ties
1:30 pm — First look and private couple portraits
items.note: A first look front-loads photos so you can enjoy cocktail hour later.

items.text: 2:00 pm — Wedding-party and immediate-family group photos
3:00 pm — Tuck away to freshen up as early guests start arriving
3:30 pm — Pre-ceremony music starts and ushers seat guests
4:00 pm — Ceremony begins
4:30 pm — Ceremony ends; cocktail hour starts and any remaining family photos are taken
5:30 pm — Guests move to the reception; the couple is announced in
5:45 pm — First dance
6:00 pm — Dinner is served, opening with a short welcome toast
7:00 pm — Speeches and toasts
items.note: Ask speakers to keep it to 3 to 5 minutes each and cap the total.

items.text: 7:45 pm — Cake cutting
8:00 pm — Dance floor opens with the parent dances
10:30 pm — Last dance and grand send-off
items.note: Line up sparklers, petals, or bubbles a few minutes ahead.

items.text: 11:00 pm — Vendors break down; assign someone to collect gifts, cards, and decor
items.note: Don't leave the gift and card box for the venue staff to gather.

items.text: 12+ months out: set your total budget, rough guest count, and your top 3 priorities as a couple
items.note: Agree on what you'll splurge on and what you'll skip before you spend a cent.

items.text: 11 months out: tour and book your venue and lock in the date
items.note: Popular venues book a year ahead — the date follows the venue, not the other way around.

items.text: 10 months out: book the photographer and videographer, and hire a planner if you want one
9 months out: book the caterer and start dress and suit shopping
items.note: Wedding dresses can take 6+ months to order and alter.

items.text: 8 months out: book the band or DJ, the officiant, and the florist
7 months out: order your dress, book hotel room blocks for guests, and plan the honeymoon
items.note: Reserve room blocks early so guests get a group rate.

items.text: 6 months out: send save-the-dates and start building your gift registry
items.note: Save-the-dates matter most for destination weddings and holiday-season dates.

items.text: 5 months out: order invitations, plan the ceremony, and choose your wedding party's attire
4 months out: do a cake tasting and order the cake, and buy the wedding rings
3 months out: finalize the menu, book hair and makeup, and apply for the marriage license
items.note: Check your license's validity window — many expire 30 to 90 days after issue.

items.text: 2 months out: mail the invitations with a clear RSVP date, and do a hair and makeup trial
items.note: RSVP deadline about 3 weeks before the wedding gives you time to chase stragglers.

items.text: 6 weeks out: final dress fitting, and start the seating chart
1 month out: confirm the final headcount with all vendors, make final payments, and write your vows
2 weeks out: finalize the seating chart, break in your shoes, and confirm the day-of timeline with every vendor
1 week out: pack for the honeymoon, assemble welcome bags, and delegate day-of tasks to trusted people
items.note: Give someone the vendor contact list so you're not fielding calls in your dress.

items.text: Day before: attend the rehearsal and rehearsal dinner, drop off items at the venue, and get an early night
Keep it to 15 minutes, timeboxed
items.note: A visible timer keeps everyone honest.

items.text: Same time, same place (or link), every working day
Everyone stands or stays on camera to keep it brief
Each person shares what they did yesterday
Each person shares what they're doing today
Each person names any blockers
items.note: The blockers are the real point of the meeting — surface them clearly.

items.text: Update the board or tracker before or during standup so it reflects reality
Flag blockers clearly and name who can help unblock them
Take detailed discussions offline: "let's take that after standup"
items.note: A quick parking lot keeps two people from stalling the whole team.

items.text: Note action items and their owners
Keep the focus on progress toward the sprint or team goal
Don't let it become a status report aimed at the manager
items.note: Standup is for the team to coordinate with each other, not to report upward.

items.text: Rotate or assign a facilitator to keep time and flow
Follow up on yesterday's blockers to make sure they got resolved
End with clear next steps and who's doing what
Define the meeting's purpose and the outcome you want
items.note: If you can't name a clear outcome, you may not need the meeting.

items.text: Decide whether a meeting is actually needed, or if an email or doc would do
Invite only the people who genuinely need to be there
items.note: Every extra attendee lowers the odds of a decision and raises the cost.

items.text: Write an agenda and share it ahead of time
Set a clear start and end time, and keep it as short as it can be
Assign a facilitator to run it and a note-taker to capture decisions
Send any pre-reads or materials in advance
items.note: Reading time inside the meeting is wasted group time.

items.text: Book the room or set up and share the video link
Test the AV, screen sharing, and any demo beforehand
Prepare your slides, data, or demo
List the specific decisions that must be made in the meeting
Come with a proposed recommendation, not just open questions
items.note: It's faster to react to a proposal than to build one from scratch live.

items.text: Plan time for discussion and for agreeing next steps
Keep a parking lot for off-topic items so they don't derail the agenda
Know who owns following up on the action items afterward
Before day 1: confirm the signed offer, contract, and start details
Before day 1: set up their email, accounts, and hardware — laptop, badge, and logins
items.note: Nothing kills day-one momentum like waiting on IT for a login.

items.text: Before day 1: prepare their desk, or ship equipment ahead for a remote start
Before day 1: assign a buddy or mentor and share a first-week schedule
items.note: A go-to peer for small questions speeds up ramp-up more than any doc.

items.text: Day 1: welcome them, give an office or virtual tour, and introduce the team
Day 1: complete HR paperwork, tax forms, and payroll setup
Day 1: review the role, expectations, and 30/60/90-day goals
Day 1: grant system access and walk through the key tools they'll use
Week 1: set up recurring 1:1s with their manager and key teammates
Week 1: share team docs, processes, and communication norms
items.note: Point them to where things live: the wiki, channels, and who owns what.

items.text: Week 1: assign a small, achievable first task to build early momentum
Week 1: complete required training and any compliance or security modules
Week 1: add them to relevant meetings, channels, and mailing lists
First month: check in regularly and ask for their early feedback
items.note: A fresh hire spots onboarding gaps you've stopped noticing.

items.text: First month: review the 30-day goals together and adjust
First month: introduce them to cross-functional partners they'll work with
First month: confirm benefits enrollment is complete
First month: run a 30-day onboarding review to see how they're settling in
Define the project goal, scope, and success criteria
items.note: Write down what's explicitly out of scope, too — that's where scope creep starts.

items.text: Identify the stakeholders and, crucially, the single decision-maker
items.note: One clear owner of the final call prevents deadlock later.

items.text: Confirm the budget and the resources you actually have
Assemble the team and confirm each person's availability
Define roles and responsibilities so ownership is unambiguous
items.note: A simple RACI (who's responsible, accountable, consulted, informed) works well.

items.text: Gather and document the requirements
Break the work into milestones and a realistic timeline
Identify dependencies and risks, and note a mitigation for each
Choose your tools for tracking, docs, and communication
Set up the project workspace: the board, repo, or shared folder
Agree on a communication cadence and how status gets reported
Define what done looks like for the first milestone
Schedule the kickoff meeting and send an agenda in advance
Run the kickoff: align on goals, plan, roles, and next steps
items.note: Leave the room only when everyone can state the goal in one sentence.

items.text: Document the decisions made and share the notes with everyone
Confirm the first tasks and their owners before you close the kickoff
Reliable high-speed internet, plus a backup like a phone hotspot
items.note: A hotspot saves the day when the router dies mid-call.

items.text: A dedicated desk or workspace, separate from where you relax
An ergonomic, adjustable chair that supports your back
An external monitor at eye level to keep your neck neutral
items.note: The top of the screen should sit roughly at eye height.

items.text: An external keyboard and mouse
Good lighting: natural light plus a task lamp
A quality webcam and a headset with a mic for clear calls
A reliable laptop or computer that meets your job's requirements
VPN and security tools installed and configured
items.note: Ask IT for the required setup before you handle any work data.

items.text: Access to all work accounts and tools, ideally via SSO and a password manager
Communication apps set up: chat, video, and email
Cloud storage and file access configured
A tidy or virtual background for video calls
Cable management and a surge-protected power strip
Set working hours and share your availability and status
items.note: Visible hours help teammates in other time zones know when to reach you.

items.text: A shutdown routine to end the workday and protect your time off
items.note: A clear stop signal is what keeps remote work from becoming always-on.

items.text: Know who to contact for IT support
A water bottle and a plan for regular breaks
